scenes.subtitle: What it does, how it works, and a lab you can reproduce step by step

lines.say: What if you could fix a bug just by writing a comment on GitHub?
With the Claude Code GitHub Action, you type @claude in an issue, and Claude reads your code, fixes it, and pushes the change.
lines.tts: With the Claude Code GitHub Action, you type at claude in an issue, and Claude reads your code, fixes it, and pushes the change.

lines.say: This video is a lab. I'll explain how it works, then we'll set it up together on a real repository. Every file is linked in the description, so you can follow along.

scenes.chapter: What is the Claude Code Action?
scenes.heading: What is [[Claude Code Action]]?
items: A **GitHub Action** that runs Claude Code inside your repository's workflows
Mention `@claude` in an issue or pull request: Claude **reads, edits, commits** and replies
Runs on **GitHub's servers**: no laptop, no terminal needed
One workflow file + one GitHub App + one secret

card.title: .GITHUB/WORKFLOWS/CLAUDE.YML
card.code:
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  claude:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: anthropics/
          claude-code-action@v1

lines.say: So, what is the Claude Code Action?
It's a GitHub Action, an automated job that GitHub runs for you, that starts Claude Code inside your repository.
You mention @claude in an issue or a pull request. Claude reads the code, makes changes, commits them, and replies in a comment.
lines.tts: You mention at claude in an issue or a pull request. Claude reads the code, makes changes, commits them, and replies in a comment.

lines.say: It all runs on GitHub's servers. Your laptop can be closed.
And the setup is just three pieces: a workflow file, the Claude GitHub App, and one secret.

scenes.heading: Two [[modes]], picked for you

rows.label: Interactive mode
rows.text: No `prompt` input: Claude waits for **@claude** in a comment

rows.label: Automation mode
rows.text: With a `prompt`: runs on any event, like a new PR or a schedule

rows.label: Safety checks
rows.text: Only users with **write access** can trigger it; bots are blocked

scenes.banner: ✓ Same Claude Code you use locally, now inside your GitHub workflow

lines.say: The action has two modes, and it picks one from your workflow file.
Interactive mode: if you don't give it a prompt, Claude waits for someone to write @claude in a comment, then answers that request.
lines.tts: Interactive mode: if you don't give it a prompt, Claude waits for someone to write at claude in a comment, then answers that request.

lines.say: Automation mode: if you give it a prompt, it runs on its own, for example on every new pull request, or every morning.
In both modes, only people with write access can trigger it, and bots are blocked. And under the hood, it's the same Claude Code you use in your terminal.

scenes.heading: What you can [[ask it to do]]

cards.title: Fix bugs
cards.text: From an issue to a branch with the fix

cards.title: Review PRs
cards.text: Comments on the code it finds risky

cards.title: Scheduled jobs

lines.say: What can you ask it to do? Answer questions about your code, right in the issue.
Fix bugs, and build features from an issue description, then push the changes to a branch.
Review pull requests and comment on the code.
Run on a schedule, like a daily summary of commits. And run your own skills or plugins.

left.title: Use the GitHub Action
left.body:
• Small, clear bugs and tasks in issues
• Reviews on every pull request
• Recurring jobs: reports, triage
• Your team works in GitHub

right.title: Stay in your terminal
right.body:
• Big, open-ended changes
• You want to steer each step
• You need to run the app and look
• Quick experiments

lines.say: When should you use it?
Use the action for small, clearly described tasks, reviews on every pull request, and recurring jobs. Especially when your team already lives in GitHub.
Stay in your terminal for big, open-ended changes, or when you want to steer every step yourself.

scenes.heading: Lab: [[fix a bug from an issue]]

left.title: Without the action
left.body:
1. Read the issue
2. Pull the code, find the bug
3. Fix it, commit, push
4. Open a pull request

**Every bug, by hand**

right.title: With the action
right.body:
1. Comment **@claude please fix this**
2. Claude finds the cause
3. Pushes a branch with the fix
4. You open the PR, tests go green

**You review, Claude does the work**

lines.say: Here's our lab: a small shop project with a shipping bug, reported in a GitHub issue.
Normally, you read the issue, pull the code, find the bug, fix it, push, and open a pull request. By hand.
With the action, you write one comment. Claude finds the cause and pushes the fix. You just review it.
Here's the starter project. You can copy it from the GitHub link in the description.

do.text:
name: Tests
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install pytest
      - run: python -m pytest

# Project rules

- Python 3.12. Tests live in tests/ and run in CI (the Tests workflow).
- Keep fixes small: change only what the issue asks for.
- Never edit a test to make it pass. Fix the code instead.
- In your reply, explain the cause of the bug in one sentence.

FREE_SHIPPING_FROM = 50  # orders of 50 or more ship free
STANDARD_RATE = 4.99


def shipping_cost(order_total):
    """Return the shipping cost for an order total."""
    if order_total > FREE_SHIPPING_FROM:
        return 0
    return STANDARD_RATE

lines.say: shipping.py has one rule: orders of fifty dollars or more ship free. But look at this line.
lines.tts: shipping dot P Y has one rule: orders of fifty dollars or more ship free. But look at this line.

lines.say: Let's run the tests. One fails: an order of exactly fifty is still charged shipping.
The project also has a Tests workflow, so GitHub runs these tests on every push. That's how we'll prove Claude's fix works.

do.label: Runs on every push and PR

lines.say: Step one: put the project on GitHub.
I commit the files, then create a new repository with the GitHub command line, and push.

do.text: git init && git add . && git commit -m "Starter"

lines.say: You need to be an admin of the repo for the next steps. On your own repo, you are.
Step two: install the Claude GitHub App. It lets Claude comment, push branches, and work with pull requests.

rows.name: Claude
rows.desc: Lets Claude work in your repositories

lines.say: I click install, and choose only the lab repository.

do.title: Install Claude
lines: Contents · Issues · Pull requests: **read and write**

lines.say: Claude mainly needs read and write access to contents, issues and pull requests. The app asks for a few more permissions, used by other Claude features.
Tip: there's also a shortcut. Run slash install-github-app inside Claude Code, and it does steps two to four for you. Here, we do it by hand, so you see every piece.

do.title: Quick setup (optional)
lines: It installs the app, saves the secret,
and opens a pull request with the workflow.

lines.say: Step three: add a secret, so the action can log in to Claude.
With a Pro or Max subscription, run claude setup-token. It creates a long-lived token for your subscription.
Then I save it as a repository secret named CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, and paste the token when asked.
lines.tts: Then I save it as a repository secret named CLAUDE CODE OAUTH TOKEN, and paste the token when asked.

out: ✓ Set Actions secret CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for you/claude-action-lab

lines.say: Secrets are encrypted by GitHub. The workflow can use them, but nobody can read them back. Not even you.
Prefer an API key from the Claude Console? Name the secret ANTHROPIC_API_KEY instead.
lines.tts: Prefer an API key from the Claude Console? Name the secret ANTHROPIC API KEY instead.

lines.say: Step four: add the workflow file. This is the heart of the setup.
Workflows live in dot github slash workflows. I call this one claude.yml.
lines.tts: Workflows live in dot github, slash workflows. I call this one claude dot yaml.

do.text:
name: Claude Code
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
  pull_request_review_comment:
    types: [created]

lines.say: The on section says when it runs: every new comment, on an issue, or on a pull request review.
This if line skips every comment that doesn't mention @claude, so you don't waste runner minutes.
lines.tts: This if line skips every comment that doesn't mention at claude, so you don't waste runner minutes.

do.text:
jobs:
  claude:
    if: contains(github.event.comment.body, '@claude')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

lines.say: Permissions: write access to contents, pull requests and issues, so Claude can push and comment. Id-token is needed to log in as the Claude app. And actions read lets Claude see your CI results.

do.text:
permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
      id-token: write
      actions: read

lines.say: The checkout step gives Claude a copy of your code to work on.
And here's the action itself: anthropics slash claude-code-action, version one.

do.text:
- uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          claude_code_oauth_token: ${{ secrets.CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN }}
          claude_args: "--max-turns 10"

lines.say: It reads the token from our secret. Never paste the token itself in this file.

do.label: From the secret, not plain text

lines.say: Claude args passes normal Claude Code options. Max turns ten caps how much work one run can do, which keeps costs under control.
There's no prompt line. So this is interactive mode: it waits for @claude.
lines.tts: There's no prompt line. So this is interactive mode: it waits for at claude.

lines.say: I commit the workflow and push it. Workflows only run once they're on GitHub.

do.text: git add . && git commit -m "Add Claude workflow" && git push

cards.title: Write a CLAUDE.md
cards.text: Your rules, read on every run. Keep it short.

cards.title: Secrets only
cards.text: Never put a token or key in the YAML

cards.title: Automate with prompt
cards.text: Add `prompt:` to run on PRs or a cron schedule

cards.title: Review before merge
cards.text: Claude pushes branches; you decide what lands

lines.say: Before you go, five tips.
One: write a CLAUDE.md. Claude reads it on every run, so keep it short and specific.
lines.tts: One: write a CLAUDE dot M D. Claude reads it on every run, so keep it short and specific.

lines.say: Two: cap every run, with max turns, and a timeout on the job. Each run uses GitHub Actions minutes, and Claude usage.
Three: keep tokens and keys in secrets. Never in the workflow file.
Four: add a prompt input, and the same action runs on its own, on every pull request, or on a schedule. The examples folder of the action's repo has ready-made workflows.
And five: Claude pushes to branches. You still review and merge.
